Volkswagen’s new ID. Polo took the overall title of “German Car of the Year 2027,” starting at just €24,995 ($28,000).
Volkswagen ID. Polo takes German Car of the Year 2027
After winning in its class among entry-level models (up to €25,000), the VW ID. Polo beat out strong international competition to take the top spot as German Car of the Year for 2027 among all vehicles.
The Volkswagen Group has won two years in a row with a compact EV. Last year, it was the Skoda Elroq.
Volkswagen opened orders for the ID. Polo with the 52 kWh battery at the end of April. In July, it added the entry-level model with the 37 kWh battery, starting at just €24,995 ($28,000) with a WLTP range of up to 207 miles (334 km).
Advertisement - scroll for more content
The Life and Style variants are also available with the 37 kWh battery, starting from €29,195 ($32,500).
With DC fast charging speeds of up to 90 kW, the ID. Polo with the 37 kWh battery can recharge from 10% to 80% in about 23 minutes.
VW Brand CEO Thomas Schäfer, VW Group Head Designer Andreas Mindt, and VW tech boss Kai Grünitz after the VW ID. Polo won German Car of the Year 2027 (Source: Thomas Schäfer)
The prestigious award “confirms what the ID. Polo stands for,” VW brand CEO Thomas Schäfer said. He added the entry-level EV “brings electric mobility to where it can make the greatest impact: right into people’s everyday lives.”
Since orders opened at the end of April, Schäfer said “well over 50,000 people have ordered their ID. Polo.”
As the first of what the company calls “a true Volkswagen again,” the ID. Polo is the first to bear an established name and the brand’s new Pure Positive design language.
Volkswagen ID. Polo (Source: Volkswagen)
The jury includes nearly 50 German and international auto journalists, and the award is considered one of the most prestigious in the industry.
In other segments, electric cars swept the awards, with the Kia PV5 van winning in the compact class (€25,000 and €40,000), and Mercedes-Benz GLC Electric taking the top spot in the premium segment (€40,000 to €70,000). Hyundai’s electric sports car, the IONIQ 6 N, won German Performance Car 2027.
Volkswagen ID. Polo interior (Source: Volkswagen)
Martin Sander, the Group’s sales boss, said earlier this month the company is “seeing a significantly accelerated trend towards all-electric vehicles” in its home market.
VW Group’s Electric Urban Car Family has received nearly 150,000 orders after series production began in June. The lineup currently includes the VW ID. Polo and ID. Cross, plus the Cupra Raval and Skoda Epiq, all based on the MEB+ platform.
While those in the US won’t see the entry-level ID. Polo, Volkswagen is set to launch the ID. Tiguan in early 2027 as a replacement for the ID.4.

Frostwarden Bronco Packs Ford's New 1,200-HP Megazilla 2.0 Supercharged 7.3L Crate Engine
21 photos
Photo: Ford
Following the original Megazilla, which builds on the Godzilla that Ford offers in the Super Duty line of trucks, the Dearborn-based automaker has finally published the maximum output figures of the Megazilla 2.0 crate engine. Frostwarden is the name of the first vehicle to put the Megazilla 2.0 to good use, with FoMoCo confirming more than 1,200 horsepower on race fuel.
Its peak torque rating exceeds 1,000 pound-feet (1,356 Newton-meters), which is good enough to impress diesel workhorses. For reference, the punchiest turbo diesel currently available in the heavy-duty truck segment is officially rated at a ludicrous 1,200 pound-feet (1,627 Newton-meters).
Beyond the Whipple supercharger, the Megazilla 2.0 wouldn't have been possible without a stronger block, upgraded pistons, a different cam, and larger fuel injectors. Ford also claims a different belt drive and damper, making the supercharged lump a different animal from the naturally aspirated Megazilla that bears part number M-6007-MZ73 in the Ford Racing Parts catalog.
Megazilla 1.0 currently retails at $25,295 via Ford Racing Parts, yet pricing for the supercharged alternative remains a mystery for now. In any case, double the horsepower and close to 50 percent more torque should make the Megazilla 2.0 a fair bit pricier.
Megazilla 2.0 was previewed in January 2025, when the Dearborn-based manufacturer was targeting more than 1,000 horsepower. As ever, the force-fed V8 is described as a competition engine rather than a regular production unit. Ford has yet to publish the maximum output figures on premium-grade fuel.
Photo: Ford The naturally aspirated Megazilla 1.0 requires premium rather than 87 octane for the Godzilla. With 93 in the tank, it makes 612 horsepower and 670 pound-feet (908 Newton-meters) of twist. Frostwarden, meanwhile, is more than simply a Bronco with a large V8 under its hood.
Frostwarden is better described as a heavy-duty overlander with Arctic truck influences. Kincer Chassis handled the build with Ford Racing Parts, Ford's engineering department, and some aftermarket partners that include BFGoodrich for the rubber, Weld for the bead-lock wheels, Dana for the driveline parts, and Bilstein for the dampers.
74Weld portal gear lifts also need mentioning, and those portal gears deserve our collective attention. Beyond providing clearance for large tires without jacking the vehicle's body too high into the air, portals keep the factory steering and suspension geometry intact.
They also widen the track to improve overall stability, hence the custom flares of this SEMA-bound thriller. Ford still doesn't offer a V8 in the Bronco. Instead, the 2027 model year saw the 2.7-liter EcoBoost's dismissal in favor of a detuned 3.0-liter EcoBoost twin-turbo V6.
Ford's only sixth-gen Bronco to feature V8 muscle is the DR , specifically a limited-run model that was produced in collaboration with Multimatic. Being a dedicated off-road desert racer, the DR is not street legal due. At least one was modified for street use, and as you might already know, a plethora of US-based performance shops and tuners do V8 conversions for this generation of the Bronco.

source_document.body:
Pfizer is calling upon lessons learned from one of the first drugs ever made available on the internet—Viagra—as it commercializes a new obesity drug in China.
Pfizer is getting its first taste of the obesity business with partner Sciwind Biosciences as the weight loss drug Ecnoglutide breaks into the Chinese market. But the idea of a consumer-driven market is not new territory for the storied New York pharma, if you look back to erectile dysfunction blockbuster Viagra.
“We are learning a lot, and we are very happy that we are entering this market because I think it is cut for our capabilities,” Pfizer CEO Albert Bourla said on a third quarter earnings call Tuesday morning.
He pointed to Pfizer’s work with Viagra, the drug that took on a life of its own and—Bourla claimed—became the first drug available on the internet.
“There are a lot of similarities, people are willing to pay out of pocket for products that they value, irrelevant if they are reimbursed or not,” Bourla said. “That creates dramatically different size in the international markets.”
Pfizer snagged mainland China licensing rights to Sciwind’s GLP‑1 receptor agonist injection Ecnoglutide in February for $495 million in upfront and potential milestone payments. The drug had already been cleared for use in the Asian country, finally giving Pfizer an approved obesity product—at least in part of the world.

Pfizer Builds Global GLP-1 Strategy With up to $495M Sciwind Deal
Ecnoglutide, which Pfizer licensed from Sciwind Biosciences, is already approved in China for type 2 diabetes mellitus, and a marketing application for weight loss has been accepted by regulatory authorities in the country.

Eli Lilly and Novo have been the clear obesity leaders for several years now, despite Pfizer’s efforts—both internal and external—to gain a foothold. Pfizer fought Novo in a bidding war for Metsera in 2025, buying a pipeline of assets that are still years from the market in the U.S. But the Sciwind deal allowed Pfizer to dip its toes into the obesity world while Metsera’s assets and other projects weave through the clinic.
Filling all the categories
Ecnoglutide isn’t the first drug for which Pfizer has drawn on its Viagra experience to market, Bourla said, pointing out that self-pay customers in China can now access migraine medicines like Nurtec or COVID treatment Paxlovid. With that model a success, it was only natural for the pharma to extend it to Ecnoglutide.
Chief International Commercial Officer Alexandre de Germay said things have been going smoothly since the April launch, providing a glimpse at the market segments that Pfizer still needs to address.
“The things that we are clearly understanding is there are very different segments within these overall chronic weight management categories,” de Germay said on Pfizer’s call.
Some patients are looking to lose weight with a more “aesthetic-driven purpose,” he continued, while others have significant weight to lose. The latter group is more willing to accept the side effects that come with weight loss medications but in turn want significant efficacy, de Germay said.

“It is confirming our strategy that if we want to be successful in chronic weight management, you need to have a portfolio,” he added. “You will need to activate all those different channels and the cost of activations of those channels will be amortized across the portfolio.”
The Ecnoglutide launch also marks a pivot for Pfizer—launching a new drug in China first rather than the typically more lucrative U.S. market. Specific to the Chinese market, de Germay said the company had to pursue a diabetes indication for Ecnoglutide in order to have access to more patients via the hospital markets. That was secured at the end of October, with an indication for type 2 diabetes.
Pfizer is also awaiting a review by Chinese regulators that would provide reimbursement for Ecnoglutide for its approved indications. This is a key milestone since rival products already have access to those, de Germay said.
More to come
With the China launch underway, Pfizer still has its eyes on the global market, particularly with the products acquired with Metsera last year. Leading the charge is berobenatide, for which Pfizer is advancing 10 pivotal studies.
“Our goal is initially to establish berobenatide as a potentially best-in-class monthly subcutaneous GLP-1 for obesity, and this is globally,” said Chris Boshoff, chief scientific officer and president of R&D, during the earnings call.
Phase 3 studies have advanced in knee osteoarthritis and obstructive sleep apnea, with initial readouts expected in the coming months, Boshoff said. Pfizer is also testing whether patients can switch from one of the existing weekly injectable GLP-1s to monthly berobenatide.
Also in development is an amylin analog called PF3945, which is being tested in combination with berobenatide in a Phase 1/2a trial.

source_document.body:
Two popemobiles that will be used during Pope Leo XIV’s visit to Peru arrived on Monday from Brazil aboard a Latam Airlines Group freighter aircraft, part of a special logistics operation carried out under contract to Peru’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and in coordination with General Motors.
The two Chevrolet vehicles, weighing three tons each and specially modified with protective features such as bulletproof glass, were transported by Latam Cargo from Varacopos International Airport in São Paulo to Lima, Peru’s capital, onboard a Boeing 767-300 freighter, the airline said in a news release.
The popemobiles were manufactured at the General Motors plant in São Bernardo do Campo near São Paulo.
Pope Leo is scheduled to visit Peru from Nov. 11 to Nov. 17 as part of a 12-day journey to Latin America that will include stops in Uruguay and Argentina. The Pope is scheduled to visit four cities in Peru. During the trip, the Pope will celebrate Mass, meet with local church communities and address civil authorities, according to the Vatican.
Latam is the largest airline in South America and its freighter division operates 19 Boeing 767-300 converted cargo jets.
Due to the vehicles’ dimensions and specific characteristics, the popemobile operation required between six and eight hours of preparation on the airport ramp, as well as specialized procedures to ensure their proper handling and transportation, Latam said.
As is normal for moving vehicles, Latam had to calculate weight distribution inside the aircraft, secure the vehicles with specialized tie-down systems on cargo platforms, and use hydraulic equipment for loading. About 20 people were required on either end of the trip for loading and unloading. The shipment also required extra security protocols to be followed.

2027 Mazda3 Goes Live, US Model Gets One Manual Trim Level
14 photos
Photo: Mazda
The row-your-own crowd has had a pretty rough 2026 thus far. Volkswagen discontinued the manual from the Jetta GLI for good, while Honda is temporarily pausing Civic Si production. Over at Mazda, the manual is alive and well in the 3. There is, however, a big catch regarding the configuration.
For starters, the 2027 Mazda3 cannot be had with three pedals unless you go for the hatchback. Secondly, front-wheel drive is a must. And thirdly, prospective customers must spend $31,950 from the outset. Said price does not include destination charge, which adds $1,315 to the final price.
The 2.5 S Premium Plus 6MT with front-wheel drive slots between the 2.5 S Preferred AWD, which is $29,990 at launch, and the 2.5 S Premium Plus. The latter comes in at $33,350 before destination and options, while the range-topping 2.5 Turbo Premium Plus will set you back a cool $38,190 for the hatchback or $37,040 for the sedan.
A bit of an oddity as of this writing, the sole manual 3 available for model year 2027 does not belong to the sporty compact club. That makes the manual grade all the more interesting, especially when you remember that increasingly more automakers prefer two-pedal setups due to improved fuel economy and better acceleration figures.
Under the hood, its 2.5-liter naturally aspirated I4 makes a respectable 186 horsepower on 87-octane regular unleaded. The Premium Plus grade makes the manual-equipped hatchback a sweet daily, for it comes with LEDs fore and aft, 10.25-inch touchscreen infotainment, a heated steering wheel, the Active Driving Display, and adaptive front lighting that swivels through corners for improved visibility on winding roads.
Photo: Mazda All other grades, be they hatchback or sedan, feature a six-speed automatic that does not like to be hurried. The sedan with said tranny in 2.5 S flavor is $24,750 for model year 2027, making it a compelling buy. Even so, there are cheaper alternatives, including the 22,390-dollar K4 from Kia. Speaking of, the much fresher design from Kia boasts segment-leading rear seat legroom for 2027.
Going for the manual-equipped Mazda3 isn't something one does with their head. Putting our sensible pants on, the Preferred hatchback is a much better pick when it comes to value for money. Starting at $28,040 in the US, the Preferred brings eight-way power adjustments and memory for the driver's seat, heating for both front seats, a power moonroof, wireless charging, and a passenger-side mirror that automatically tilts down when reversing.
All-wheel drive further complicates things, with Mazda offering the Preferred hatchback with all-wheel drive from $29,990 (or $31,305 after destination). Prospective customers of the 2.5 Turbo Premium Plus with all-wheel drive get up to 250 horsepower and 320 pound-feet (434 Newton-meters) at full chatter, albeit only with 93-octane premium dino juice.
Filling it up with 87 octane drops both numbers, with Mazda claiming 227 hp and 310 lb-ft (420 Nm). Presumably due to the manual's inherent limitations, the force-fed engine is not compatible with said manual. The rest of the 2027 model year changes are concentrated on everyday equipment.
Cordless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto are now standard from the Select Sport up, which further sweetens the deal with Alexa built-in, 18-inch black alloys, dual-zone climate control, leatherette upholstery, and rain-sensing wipers. Preferred adds Qi wireless phone charging and extra comfort goodies.

The Airbus full scale Wingman model was displayed for the first time at the 2024 ILA Berlin Air Show (Photo: Breaking Defense)
MUNICH — Airbus has scrapped the development of a futuristic, unmanned wingman concept aircraft as a result of Germany accelerating the timeline for the aircraft to potentially enter service .
The European manufacturer is moving away from its Wingman drone platform , first unveiled at the Berlin Air Show in 2024 , to instead focus on developing the U760 Ravenstorm Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCA), according to Laurent Le Quément, head of future air power and UAS marketing at Airbus.
“Customers have asked us to bring the need [service entry] forward,” he told reporters here at the International Fighter Conference. “We decided to recheck our whole approach and to go for this [the U760].”
The original timeframe for fielding the Wingman was “definitely not early 2030s,” added Le Quément. At the CCA’s unveiling in 2024, Michael Schoellhorn, CEO of Airbus Defence and Space indicated that the timeline was much closer to 2040.
Though Le Quément did not identify the customer by name, Airbus stated in 2024 that the Wingman aircraft was designed specifically to meet emerging operational requirements of the German Air Force.
In light of the tighter timeline, Airbus decided to pursue development of the U760 because it is an evolution of the company’s Barracuda drone demonstrator’s “trusted design,” said Le Quément. Work on Barracuda began in 2003, initially as a secret project and subsequently led to the completion of six flight test campaigns.
One significant difference distinguishing the Wingman from the U760 is that the Wingman was to be fitted with a bespoke engine created by Rolls Royce Deutschland and Spanish engine manufacturer ITP Aero. Meanwhile, the U760 will be fitted with a business jet engine, Le Quément explained.
“If you have something which is [intended to be] affordable, you need to be at a certain ratio of a fighter,” said Le Quément. “But if you’re talking then about something … which would be bespoke for air-to-air with an AESA [Active Electronically Scanned Array] radar in there, then you would be at a much higher cost.”
Airbus was targeting an estimated cost for the Wingman equivalent to be “one third” of a manned fighter platform, per past Schoellhorn comments.
Ravenstorm offers a high subsonic cruise speed and features a 500 kg (1102.3 lbs.) internal weapons bay capacity, per Airbus literature. It is the second in a family of three CCA designs also including the U740 Valkyrie, and an unnamed third system.
Airbus displays the U760 Ravenstrom CCA at the International Fighter Conference in Munich (Breaking Defense)
The U740 Valkyrie is being developed to support a 2029 German requirement, followed by Ravenstorm’s push to enter service in 2032; and rounded off by a future design that remains under assessment.
“The third one you will not see it” today, said Le Quément, noting that the aircraft is at a study phase at present. “But the idea is to investigate more bespoke designs, which will be done either for air-to-air or for EW [electronic warfare], and that might be something which would tend to be more exquisite,” he said.
The company further provided an update on the U740 program, which involves an industry partnership with US firm Kratos.
Building off a first flight out of Northern Europe last month, the aircraft is scheduled to take part in a crewed-uncrewed teaming flight in collaboration with a Eurofighter Typhoon fourth-generation fighter jet next year, Marco Mehling, chief engineer system of systems concepts and capabilities at Airbus, told media in Munich today.
It was recently reported that Germany’s 2029 CCA requirement timeline is in doubt, after rethinking a direct procurement of Boeing MQ-28 Ghost Bat drones. The move means that competitors like Airbus, offering the Valkyrie, are still in the running to secure an order from Berlin.
“[If the] capability is used or pushed back, and they [Germany] need it in [20]32, of course, this is good for us, but we want still to be ready by the timescales that were initially mentioned”, said Mehling.

source_document.body:
An October survey of supply chain executives confirmed what truckload carriers said on recent quarterly calls—that rates are likely to remain on the rise for the foreseeable future. The Logistics Managers’ Index, released Tuesday, showed further capacity declines alongside surging pricing.
Q3 reports show carriers gearing up for big rate increases
The LMI’s transportation capacity dataset registered a reading of 38 for October, an 11th straight month in contraction, albeit at a pace that was 3.6 percentage points slower than September’s rate of decline. (The LMI is a diffusion index in which a reading above 50 indicates expansion, while one below 50 signals contraction.)
Transportation utilization (63.5) continued to increase, but at a pace that was 2.6 points slower sequentially. Upstream companies (manufacturers and wholesalers) returned a 69.3 utilization reading, which was 16 points higher than downstream retailers.
Transportation prices (88) continued “expanding at a highly significant rate,” but at a pace that was 4.7 points slower. (Diesel fuel prices were down 1% sequentially during the month, up 70% y/y.)
SONAR: Outbound Tender Rejection Index (OTRI.USA) for 2026 (blue shaded area), 2025 (yellow line), 2024 (green line) and 2023 (pink line). A proxy for truck capacity, the tender rejection index shows the number of loads being rejected by carriers. Current tender rejections show a tight truckload market. To learn more about SONAR, click here .
While cost pressures tamped down truckload carriers’ earnings in the third quarter, the group expects to capture double-digit rate increases in the upcoming bid season .
Knight-Swift Transportation ( NYSE: KNX ), which has roughly 70% of its TL fleet operating under non-dedicated agreements, is targeting “at least double-digit [rate] increases” in annual contractual negotiations that just began. The company decided to lean into the spot market earlier this year, which led to tender rejections that were two to three times higher than the industry average during the third quarter.
A widespread crackdown on noncompliant capacity has carriers betting that the recovery is just beginning. Some carriers recently said that they would look to grow their one-way fleets after years of repositioning this equipment under dedicated agreements or disposing of it altogether in order to improve asset utilization.
SONAR: Contract Rate Change Direction (CRCD.USA). The dataset measures the average percentage difference between new and former contract base rates. Recent contract renewals are averaging 13%.
Logistics managers surveyed expect the transportation market to remain very tight over the next 12 months, returning future readings of 49.3 for capacity, 67.6 for utilization and 90 for pricing. While the group now expects capacity contraction to slow over the next year (September’s outlook on capacity was 37.9), it expects transportation rates to surge faster (pricing forecast up 3.9 points sequentially).
Inventories up on hopeful holiday expectations
The overall LMI (70.7) was up 50 basis points in October to the second-highest level in over four years. June’s 71.1 reading was the highest level recorded over that period. Year-to-date, the index average is the second-highest in the dataset’s 10-year history, and approximately 9 points above last year.
October inventory levels (66.9) jumped 8 points from September, logging the fastest growth rate in four years. A 72.1 growth rate in the second half of the month was approximately 10 points higher than the first half.
“After a year of playing things very cautiously due to doubts about the consumer and the high costs of tariffs and transportation, firms are now pulling inventories in as quickly as they can – often at high costs – in an effort to capitalize on what they hope will be a blockbuster holiday season,” the report said.
Knight-Swift said it is seeing the most peak-season project freight in its network since the pandemic.
Inventory Costs (88.8) increased 8.9 points to the highest reading for the dataset since March 2022.
The change in inventories was evident in the warehousing metrics.
The rate of decline in warehouse capacity (43.5) slowed 4.2 points, but remained firmly in contraction territory. There was no change to capacity in January and February; however, the index has contracted in six of the past eight months. Upstream companies reported severe contraction (37.5) while downstream firms saw no change in space availability.
Warehouse utilization (58.8) increased at a rate that was 5.5 points slower, but warehouse prices (80.7) surged 7.2 points.
Aggregate logistics costs (inventory, warehousing and transportation) totaled 257.5, up 11.4 points sequentially, and the fastest growth rate since March 2022—the end of pandemic-fueled consumer spending and the start of the war in Ukraine. The all-in costs index was 55 points higher year over year in October.
The LMI is a collaboration among Arizona State University, Colorado State University, Florida Atlantic University, Rutgers University and the University of Nevada, Reno, conducted with the Council of Supply Chain Management Professionals.
Why it matters? The Logistics Managers’ Index provides a look at all major supply chain costs. The latest report signals a difficult operating environment for shippers characterized by limited capacity and rapidly rising costs.

source_document.body:
A federal appeals court challenge to the U.S. Unified Carrier Registration (UCR) system could disrupt annual registration fees paid by trucking companies and threaten funding for state commercial vehicle safety programs, according to the organization that administers the program.
The Small Business in Transportation Coalition (SBTC) filed a petition Oct. 20 with the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit challenging the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration ’s 2027 UCR fee rule and alleging that the registration system and its governing board were never lawfully established.
The coalition is asking the court to set aside the fee rule, halt fee collections and require federal regulators to establish the UCR system through rulemaking.
In written responses to FreightWaves, Avelino Gutierrez, executive director of the UCR Plan, acknowledged that a ruling in SBTC’s favor could have significant consequences.
“If the United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit were to set aside the 2027 fee rule and/or halt UCR fee collections, then registration operations, fee collections and the distributions of funds to the states could be greatly affected,” Gutierrez said.
He added that many states use UCR revenue directly for motor carrier safety and enforcement activities.
The lawsuit comes as registration fees for 2027 are increasing by approximately 20%, adding to operating costs for motor carriers already facing challenging freight market conditions.
SBTC challenges legal foundation of UCR system
The UCR program requires interstate motor carriers, brokers, freight forwarders and certain other transportation businesses to register annually and pay fees based on fleet size or business classification.
The program was established under federal legislation enacted in 2005, with participating states receiving revenue to support motor carrier safety and enforcement activities.
SBTC’s petition, filed as Case No. 26-1297, argues that FMCSA failed to promulgate regulations formally establishing the UCR system as required by U.S. code 49 U.S.C. §13908.
James Lamb, SBTC’s executive director, told FreightWaves that the alleged failure calls into question the legality of the governing board, registration agreement and subsequent fee rules.
“Because the UCR system was never lawfully established, the UCR Board of Directors, the UCR Agreement that the Board wrote, and every single fee rule ever set under the authority of the UCR Agreement are all illegal,” Lamb said.
The coalition also contends that the registration system should operate under greater direct federal oversight, including the handling of registration funds and truckers’ personal information.
Gutierrez rejected the coalition’s interpretation.
“Without arguing the merits of the case here, the UCR Plan strongly believes it was lawfully established under 49 U.S.C. Section 14504(a) et seq.,” he said.
FMCSA has previously defended the program’s statutory authority. In its September final rule, the agency stated that Congress established the UCR Plan and its fee-collection requirements under 49 U.S.C. §14504a.
The competing interpretations have not been resolved in the latest appeal.
Coalition seeks expedited court ruling
On Oct. 26, SBTC filed a motion seeking expedited consideration of the lawsuit, citing the approaching 2027 registration enforcement date.
Lamb said the coalition is not requesting an immediate suspension of fee collections while the case proceeds.
“We are not seeking an emergency stay but we are seeking emergency expedited merits review,” Lamb told FreightWaves.
The distinction is important for trucking companies preparing to register for 2027.
Although SBTC wants the court to invalidate the fee rule, Lamb said carriers should continue complying with existing registration requirements unless a court orders otherwise.
“If it doesn’t rule before then, carriers should pay their 2027 UCR fees by December 31st to avoid civil penalties,” Lamb said.
Gutierrez offered similar guidance.
“As neither the Court of Appeals nor any other court has ruled otherwise, the UCR Plan’s current guidance is to register for UCR prior to enforcement beginning on January 1, 2027,” he said.
Registration for 2027 opened Oct. 1 through the UCR Plan’s website.
The new petition follows an earlier SBTC challenge to FMCSA’s handling of the UCR system. Lamb said the D.C. Circuit’s June denial of an earlier request to pause rulemaking did not resolve the merits of the coalition’s legal arguments.
Dispute extends to truckers’ personal information
Beyond the fee rule, SBTC is challenging what it alleges is improper disclosure of truckers’ personally identifiable information, including Social Security numbers, to the UCR system and its technology contractor.
Lamb said he discovered a vulnerability in 2019 after finding that his own Social Security number had been exposed through the UCR registration website.
The coalition has since asked the U.S. Department of Transportation ’s Office of Inspector General to investigate FMCSA’s data-sharing practices and the security of the UCR website.
In an Oct. 13 complaint, SBTC requested an audit of the system’s information technology infrastructure and compliance with federal privacy requirements.
Gutierrez disputed the suggestion that Social Security numbers are currently being transferred to the UCR Plan.
“Personally identifiable information, including social security numbers, has not been given by FMCSA to the UCR Plan since March 2019,” he said.
Gutierrez acknowledged a 28-day exposure in March 2019 when some tax identification numbers corresponding to Social Security numbers appeared in the browser status bar associated with registration receipts.
“The UCR Plan does not solicit nor receive PII from any entity, government or otherwise,” he said.
A UCR investigation released after the incident identified approximately 30,000 registrant accounts potentially exposed to the vulnerability. Of those, approximately 23,000 may have used Social Security numbers as tax identification numbers.
The UCR Plan said at the time that it found no indication of a mass export of the information, corrected the vulnerability and arranged notifications and identity-monitoring services for potentially affected registrants.
SBTC maintains that the historical incident and the program’s data-sharing arrangements warrant further federal scrutiny. The coalition’s allegations of ongoing Privacy Act violations remain disputed.
What’s at stake for trucking companies?
The case presents two distinct potential consequences for the trucking industry.
For motor carriers, brokers and owner-operators, a court ruling against the UCR system could create uncertainty over future registration requirements and the collection of annual fees.
For participating states, a suspension of collections could affect revenue used for roadside inspections, commercial vehicle enforcement and other motor carrier safety activities.
Gutierrez cautioned that the extent of any disruption would depend on the court’s ruling.
SBTC, meanwhile, maintains that its goal is to bring the registration program into compliance with federal law rather than permanently eliminate safety funding.
The coalition is also pursuing a separate complaint alleging improper use of UCR funds for a planned March 2027 board meeting in Florida.
Why it matters: A ruling against the UCR system could affect registration obligations for trucking companies, brokers and other transportation businesses while jeopardizing revenue used by states for commercial vehicle safety enforcement.

PARIS — Today Britain’s BAE Systems debuted a new series of naval guns designed to tackle airborne, surface, and shore threats at the Euronaval defense show in Paris.
The family of guns is derived from the Bofors 40 Mk4 naval gun that first started development more than 15 years ago. Each of the three variants come with their own characteristics, all designed around trying to meet the needs of modern navies, according to the firm.
“The maritime threat landscape is evolving rapidly, creating a growing need for flexible and effective protection solutions,” Lena Gillström, president of BAE Systems Bofors, said in a news release. “With the Sea Tridon, navies and maritime operators can select the capability level that best meets their operational needs while benefiting from a common platform, proven technology and advanced programmable ammunition.”
The three variants are:
Sea Tridon, which combines the Bofors 40mm gun with an “integrated electro-optical fire-control system” that the company says will make it easier to integrate onto new platforms.
Sea TridonC, a containerized version of the Sea Tridon. Militaries around the world have been experimenting with containerized systems , which can be swiftly deployed and, if needed, abandoned after use.
Sea Trinity, which the company claims is the “most advanced” of the family. It comes with the Bofars 40mm gun and integrated fire control radar, and is specifically to be used to counter the kind of small missiles and drones that have come to represent major threats to ships in the Black Sea and the Gulf.
Speaking to reporters at the show, Stefan Lofstrom, BAE Systems Bofors director of marketing and sales, emphasized that the new systems will use the company’s already in-production ammunition.
“Ammunition-wise, all those variants are compatible with our programmable 3P ammunition,” Lofstrom told reporters at Euronaval. “That’s been around on the market for a long time. It’s well proven, again. That’s really the unique selling point with these systems: the 3P ammunition.”
Lofstrom said that conversations are also underway with “several navies” right now about the integration of the Sea Tridon guns on unmanned systems that would go out to sea without human support for weeks at a time, in order to work out how certain aspects like gun maintenance and ammunition reloading could be handled without crew aboard.
Customers for BAE’s Mk4 naval gun already include the UK’s Royal Navy and the Royal Netherlands Navy, who have purchased the weapon for some of their frigates. Additionally, the Royal Netherlands Navy and the Belgian Navy, among others, have selected the naval gun for their mine countermeasure vessels.
“The starting point for this family of new products is the existing customer base, but then we, in parallel, have ongoing customer conversations with I would say a handful or two handfuls of customers,” Lofstrom said. “We don’t have a launch customer for [the Sea Tridon family] yet, but we have some advanced discussions with different customers.”

This DIY Bus Conversion Is a Stunning Roving Home With Warm Styling, Moss Walls, and Three Skylights
25 photos
Photo: Mobile Dwellings/YouTube screenshot
Turning an old vehicle into a mobile home with no prior building experience is no easy task, and the idea might even seem impossible at first, but there are plenty of stories out there that prove it is entirely achievable. DIY projects like this bus home built by Ryan and Lyss, a travel-loving couple from Colorado, show that the lack of experience should not hinder you from achieving your dreams.
After spending six months backpacking through Southeast Asia, Ryan and Lyss wanted to continue living a more adventurous lifestyle, so they decided to build a skoolie and use it as their rocking home as they travel across the US.
Neither of them had any prior building experience, but they took on the challenge and learned along the way, and the result of their hard work is impressive to say the least. It’s not just a simple place to crash out after a day of adventuring but a proper tiny home on wheels fitted with all the comforts of a conventional home, practical amenities, and beautiful styling.
Ryan and Lyss’s bus home is based on a 1999 Blue Bird TC2000, a 26-foot (7.9-meter) long, front-engine school bus. This particular size is considered rare and highly sought-after among skoolie enthusiasts. Powered by a 5.9-liter Cummins engine paired with an Allison transmission, the bus was in overall good condition when they bought it.
Photo: Mobile Dwellings/YouTube screenshot This allowed them to get down to work and transform it into a comfortable and practical living space with everything they needed. Though characterized by minimalism, the interior is warm and inviting, with lots of windows, a neutral color palette, potted plants, and cozy textural linen and curtains that all help create the calm and serene ambiance of a proper home.
They describe the interior styling as “Tulum meets industrial,” as they combined natural materials and earthy tones with contemporary finishes. They used a lot of microcement to ground the design, including on the walls, the furniture bases, bathroom surfaces, and even on the countertops. Because it flows across multiple surfaces, the material creates a sense of visual continuity, making the bus’s interior feel larger, while the neutral beige color makes it feel calm and organic. A slatted ceiling with integrated LED lighting adds even more warmth to the design.
Plants and greenery are also abundant inside this bus, so the couple made sure the interior would receive plenty of natural light. Apart from the bus’s windows, the couple installed three skylights - a large one above the main living area and two smaller ones over the rear bed.
Photo: Mobile Dwellings/YouTube screenshot Though this Blue Bird is a shorter bus , the interior space has been efficiently utilized to include a cozy lounge, a dedicated sleeping area, a stylish bathroom, and a function kitchen equipped with modern conveniences.
At the front, the living room and kitchen kind of blend into one open space, with a custom L-shaped sofa providing the main seating area. The sofa hides all the components of the power system underneath, and it also pulls into a guest bed when needed.
Lyss loves to cook, so even if the kitchen is compact, she wanted to make sure it provided all the functionality she needed to practice her cooking skills. So they equipped it with a glass-covered four-burner cooktop, a full-size oven, a farmhouse sink, and an apartment-size fridge. There are enough drawers and cabinets for storage, and the microcement countertop extends over a front cabinet to provide more workspace for cutting and chopping.
The kitchen also includes a moss wall that Lyss plans to eventually grow into a herb garden, as well as a pull-out pantry and trash cans.
Photo: Mobile Dwellings/YouTube screenshot At the back, the bedroom and bathroom share the width of the bus, with a half-wall separating the two areas. The bedroom is very simple but cozy, with a built-in bed over a large garage area and some wall niches. The garage area also houses their dog’s bed.
Two skylights above this rear area bring in natural light both in the bedroom and the bathroom, and a built-in planter box on the division wall holds plants that hang down on both sides, adding a nice, natural touch.
The bathroom is designed as a small oasis, with microcement covering the walls and ceiling and petrified wood tiles adding texture to the floor. The space is fitted with a full shower, a toilet cleverly tucked under the shower bench, built-in open shelves, and a mirror and moss wall.
Photo: Mobile Dwellings/YouTube screenshot This bus home also has a huge closet, a second entrance door, a full-size mirror next to it, a dedicated bookshelf, plenty of hidden storage, and other practical features that make full-time living on the road easier.
On the outside, instead of a simple layer of paint, the couple decided to apply Raptor protective coating on the entire bus, ensuring the exterior benefits from a protective barrier that can withstand the toughest situations. They applied the coating themselves and chose a light tan finish.
On top of the bus, they installed a custom roof rack that holds an impressive solar array (1,600 watts of solar panels), along with perimeter light bars for excellent visibility wherever they are parked. The bus is also fitted with security cameras and an exterior speaker.
Photo: Mobile Dwellings/YouTube screenshot The couple doesn’t tow a vehicle but they do have a Royal Enfield Himalayan motorcycle that they take along on their travels. To carry it, they installed a motorcycle rack from MotoTote with a removable ramp.
A 1,600-watt solar array on the roof, paired with two Lithionics 24V 200Ah batteries, takes care of the bus’s energy needs in off-grid locations, and for heating and hot water, Ryan and Lyss opted for the Timberline hydronic system from Elwell Corporation. The system provides space heating and on-demand hot water and can run on either diesel or electricity.
It took Ryan and Lyss about a year and a half to complete their DIY bus home, during which they also lived in the bus. The total cost of the conversion was around $60,000, including the materials, equipment, and all the tools they needed to work on it.

Tesla’s driver-assistance system in Europe can no longer be set to drive 50% over the speed limit. The Netherlands’ RDW, which approved the system in April, confirmed today that it signed off on an update capping the speed margin at 10% and officially renaming “FSD Supervised” to Tesla Assisted Driving.
The changes land weeks before EU member states could vote on approving the system across the bloc, and they match the conditions Germany set last month.
The RDW confirms the 50% setting
The RDW’s notice is the clearest official confirmation of how the system was configured when the Dutch regulator approved FSD Supervised on April 10 . The “speed margin,” which lets the system deviate from the detected limit for “safety and traffic flow,” could go up to +50%. On a 100 km/h highway, that’s 150 km/h. In a 30 km/h city zone, it’s 45 km/h.
Now the margin tops out at +10%. It also resets to 0% every time the car starts, and the RDW says other speed-related functions are now disabled by default. It didn’t say which ones.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
The new name shows up on the in-car display, in the owner’s manual, and in other driver information on HW4 vehicles. Tesla pushes all of it over the air.
“Minor changes”
The RDW describes the update as “several minor changes” that Tesla asked it to assess. The regulator says it checked the implementation, found no adverse or unintended effects, and folded the changes into the existing type approval without amending or extending it. It also stresses that the rename doesn’t change what the system does. It’s still driver assistance, and the driver is still responsible.
The RDW notified the nine member states that recognize its approval: Belgium, Croatia, Czechia, Denmark, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Slovakia, and Slovenia. That’s 10 countries counting the Netherlands, up from eight at the start of October.
The EU-wide decision still sits with the Technical Committee on Motor Vehicles (TCMV). The RDW says those talks are confidential and won’t comment on them. As we reported, the EU pushed the vote to December at the earliest , and passing it takes a qualified majority: 15 of 27 member states representing at least 65% of the EU population.
Speeding was the main objection
Speed has been the biggest problem for Tesla’s file in Brussels. In June, Sweden asked the EU to reject FSD unless Tesla removed the ability to set speeds above the posted limit. In September, a Brussels pedestrian safety group found the system speeding in 55% of the 30 km/h segments it tested , in a country that had already approved it. France has cited urban speeding as one of its reasons for refusing to recognize the Dutch approval.
Then, on October 6, Germany’s Transport Ministry said it would back EU approval after Tesla agreed to drop the “Full Self-Driving” name, which the ministry called misleading, and to cap speed tolerance at 10%. Today’s RDW update delivers both.
But 10% isn’t what Sweden asked for. Sweden wanted no setting above the limit at all. Several European countries are known for enforcing speed limits strictly.
Electrek’s Take
Good, but that’s only part of the problem. Tesla’s biggest issue with FSD right now is that it doesn’t properly detect the speed limits.
Being locked at 10% over the limit doesn’t mean much if you don’t know the actual limit.
The name change is needed globally and it is past due. “Tesla Assisted Driving” describes what the system does. Meanwhile, Tesla still sells the exact same kind of software in the US as “Full Self-Driving (Supervised)” for $99 a month. If it’s misleading in Berlin, it’s misleading in California.
Practically, this update gets Tesla Germany’s vote. The question for December is whether a 10% cap is enough for France, Italy, and Spain, or whether Sweden’s zero-tolerance line wins out.

Hyundai IONIQ 5 sales rebound in October
While the Tesla Model Y and Model 3 still dominate the US electric vehicle market, accounting for about 50% of all sales through the third quarter , it was the Hyundai IONIQ 5 that ranked third.
The market has slowed since the $7,500 federal tax credit was removed last September, with several automakers reporting fewer EV sales than in 2025 when buyers rushed to claim the credit.
Hyundai responded by cutting prices on the 2026 IONIQ 5 by up to nearly $10,000 on some trims, with a new starting MSRP of around $35,000.

As the market shows signs of recovery, IONIQ 5 sales bounced back in October, rising 21% to 1,981 units.
Through the first 10 months of 2026, Hyundai sold 33,093 IONIQ 5s in the US, still down 23% from the more than 42,700 it sold during the same period last year, when credit was still available.
2027 Hyundai IONIQ 5 (Source: Hyundai)
Hyundai said the IONIQ 5 helped drive growth as the company posted its best October in the US ever with 73,452 vehicles sold, a 5% increase YOY.
While Hyundai sold only 169 IONIQ 9s last month (-47%), sales are still up 49% through October, with nearly 6,700 units sold.
2027 Hyundai IONIQ 5 interior (Source: Hyundai)
Hyundai’s hybrids set a new October sales record, rising 20% from last year and accounting for 29% of total sales in October. Through October, Hyundai’s total US sales are up 3% YOY at 770,916 units.
Since not all automakers report monthly sales figures, it’s hard to determine where the IONIQ 5 stands through October.
2027 Hyundai IONIQ 5 interior (Source: Hyundai)
Earlier today, Hyundai’s sister brand Kia reported that sales of its three-row electric SUV, the EV9, were up 11% year over year in October. EV9 sales are now up 5% year-to-date, with 13,835 units sold through October.

2026 SEMA Show • Ringbrothers Mesmerizes the SEMA Show Once Again, This Time With Billie, the 650-HP Pontiac GTO
Rare 1973 GTO Lying in State in Upstate New York Field, Wouldn't You Like a Peak Under Its Hood?
21 photos
Photo: YouTube/Steve Magnante
Automotive history is riddled with “What Ifs” that simply don’t allow certain gearheads to sleep peacefully, and incessantly ponder about what the landscape would’ve been had one decision been (or not) made. In retrospective, what would’ve become of the GTO if Pontiac had actually made it with the Super Duty? We’ll never have that version of reality, but this field-find 1973 GTO would probably have been a much more valued machine today.
“Hold on,” you might say, “Pontiac retired the Super Duty before the GTO was a thing.” Yes, and they brought it back ten years later. With that horror decision from January 1963 to withdraw all GM divisions from factory-backed racing, the corporation effectively strapped a naval canon on its hip, and pulled the trigger, while aiming at its own foot. It didn’t miss.
Ever the rebels, Pontiac’s brainiacs wrenchers didn’t back down. Instead, they developed the GTO. Which was the perfect middle finger to yet another corporate decision to ban engines with a lower ratio than ten lb of car weight per cubic inch of displacement from being installed as standard in intermediates. Meaning that all mid-sizers could have a 400-cube at the most.
“Standard” was the key word that allowed Pontiac to drill the perfect loophole: the commandment said nothing about optional muscle. Armed with the lessons learned from the Super Duty racing program of the early sixties, Pontiac built a 389 with special-purpose parts, put it in the LeMans, and called it a Gran Turismo Omologato.
Photo: YouTube/Steve Magnante The muscle car was born. By 1972, it was dead or dying. Not from Pontiac, not even from GM – from everyone. After spawning a horsepower war like never before, Pontiac had to bury the GTO because… well, who cares why? Insurance premiums, emission-compliance rules, buyer boredom – you name it. it was a mass extinction similar in amplitude with the disappearance of the megafauna of the ice age.
The super-predators and oversized beasts were driven into oblivion, one by one. Pontiac had every honest intention of fighting to the last bullet and man standing, but the writing was on the wall, and the wall was the great wall of China, and the letters were skyscraper-sized. But they gave it their best shot, nonetheless.
During the golden era of Detroit horsepower, General Motors permitted Buick, Oldsmobile, and Pontiac to engineer completely distinct 455-cubic-inch (7.5-liter) V8 engines (Chevrolet had one ideas, settling for only 454 inches. And 450 horsepower. Talks about the baddest MF’ers in town). Pontiac created its big-bore powerhouse by punching out the earlier 428-cubic-inch design, culminating in the headline news for the 1973 model year, the ferocious 455-cubic-inch Super Duty.
Photo: YouTube/Steve Magnante Although intended as the ultimate engine for the 1973 GTO, the hand-assembled powerplant never reached showroom buyers in that intermediate. It made the Firebird a superpower and a legend, and that was it.
Engineered to defy tightening regulations, the Super Duty 455 featured four-bolt main caps, screw-in oil plugs, dry-sump lubrication provisions, a nodular iron crankshaft, forged steel rods with 7/16-inch bolts, and forged aluminum pistons. Topped by flow-bench-designed cylinder heads, a high-lift camshaft, big headers, and a revamped Quadrajet four-barrel carburetor fed by functional Ram Air scoops, it delivered 310 net horsepower on 91-octane fuel, promising the greatest muscle car ever.
So great, in fact, that it actually won the Performance Car of the Year from Hi-Performance Cars magazine. There was, however, one slight issue: by the time the media outlet released its verdict, Pontiac axed the Super Duty from the GTO. The publication was left hanging, but Pontiac had actually advertised the 455 SD for the 1973 LeMans GTO in its brochures in the preamble to the model year lineup.
Photo: YouTube/Steve Magnante Pontiac built a trio of pre-production Super Duty 455 GTOs, comprising two Muncie M-20 4-speed manuals and a solitary Turbo Hydra-Matic 3-speed automatic. There was also a Grand Am for magazine evaluations. Testers like Joe Oldham raved about its flat cornering, 1.125-inch front and 1-inch rear sway bars, and G60-15 tires.
However, federal regulators discovered an unapproved emissions vacuum delay valve, and after noise-test delays, management killed the $578 engine option for all intermediate models. That cancellation arrived near the twilight of a storied badge that spanned 14 model years and five distinct generations, accumulating 555,538 total units.
The classic run lasted 11 years from 1964 through 1974 across four generations, totaling 514,793 cars, before a fifth-generation Australian-built revival added 40,745 coupes across 3 years from 2004 through 2006. Across the 5 years (‘64-’65 and ’72-‘74) offered strictly as an option package, Pontiac assembled 125,473 examples in total.
Photo: YouTube/Steve Magnante Introduced during the first generation as a Tempest LeMans option package, the GTO recorded 32,450 sales in 1964 and 75,352 in 1965, totaling 107,802 early package cars. Becoming a standalone model, output reached 96,946 units in 1966 and 81,722 in 1967. The second generation brought 87,684 cars in 1968, 72,287 in 1969, 40,149 in 1970, and 10,532 in 1971, before reverting to a LeMans package with 5,807 built in 1972.
The third generation arrived for a 1-year run in 1973 on the Colonnade A-body platform, reaching an all-time low of 4,806 GTO-packaged cars. In 1974, the fourth generation shifted to the compact X-body Ventura with a 200-horsepower, 350-cubic-inch V8, tallying 7,058 units and bringing the 1972 through 1974 package total to 17,671 cars.
For 1973, the GTO remained a $368 option package rather than model, offered on two body-on-frame Colonnade hardtop body styles. Buyers could apply the package to the base LeMans coupe, which accounted for 494 units, or the LeMans Sport Coupe with louvered rear quarter windows, which attracted 4,312 of the 4,806 orders. Depending on base V8 trim, the complete GTO carried a starting price between $3,376 and $3,775.
Photo: YouTube/Steve Magnante The package bundled a blacked-out grille, dual NASA hood scoops, Moon-styled hubcaps on 7-inch-wide wheels, chrome dual exhausts, and heavy-duty suspension. Standard power came from the T-code 400-cubic-inch (6.6-liter – or litre, because that’s how Detroit spelled metrics back then) four-barrel V8 producing 230 net horsepower and 325 pound-feet of torque.
That base motor was installed in 4,262 cars with a 3- and 4-speed manual, or a 3-speed Turbo Hydra-Matic automatic. Only 544 buyers chose the 250-horsepower, 370-lb-ft 455-cubic-inch V8, all built as automatics.
Equipped with the 230-horsepower 400 V8 or the 250-horsepower 455 V8, period tests recorded 0 to 60 mph sprints between 7.6 and 8.2 seconds and quarter-mile runs around 15.6 seconds. Dismal numbers by all standards, both contemporary or historically comparative, even probably junk enough to kick a GTO out in a field. Literally.
Photo: YouTube/Steve Magnante Automotive historian Steve Magnante recently spotlighted a surviving example on his YouTube channel, in the brush of West Lebanon, New York. The car is one of the 4,312 LeMans Sport Coupe GTOs featuring plastic rear quarter-window louvers installed over the rear side windows. Up front, its impact-absorbing chrome bumper and flexible urethane filler panel, engineered to rebound within 24 hours after a 5-mph impact, sit below plastic grilles housing aftermarket yellow day-2 driving lights.
Non-factory plastic covers shield the single round headlamps, while peeling black paint on the streamlined teardrop tail shows the coupe was originally painted blue. Although the one-year-only NACA-scoop hood is rusted shut, peering through the openings reveals the original T-code 400 V8, upgraded with an Edelbrock intake manifold, finned aluminum Mickey Thompson valve covers, and an open-element air cleaner, complemented outside by N50-15 tires on American Racing Vector wheels.
Photo: YouTube/Steve Magnante Inside the burgundy cabin, this unusual cruiser pairs a front bench seat and column-shifted 3-speed automatic transmission with a factory non-tachometer gauge cluster and remote metal driver mirror. This engine-transmission-body combo was the most common GTO of 1973: a LeMans Sport with a 400 automatic saw 2,867 copies ordered, out of the 4,807 total GTO-equipped Pontiacs.
Period Day 2 modifications continue indoors with a Grant GT steering wheel, a column-mounted Stewart-Warner tachometer, and finned aluminum window cranks. Framed by GTO-exclusive rectangular taillights and dual exhausts, this weathered New York would probably abandon its spot at the waiting line to the pearly gates of the crusher, if someone were to drag it out and breathe the breath of life into its NACA hood ducts.

The French navy ship, the FS Languedoc (D653), as seen in port on January 20, 2024 in Djibouti, Djibouti. (Luke Dray/Getty Images)
PARIS — France’s Minister of the Armed Forces says the country’s military ambition to be “feared” on the global stage is driving major modernization investments, including naval drone and munitions programs.
“This ambition reflects a firmly established French political determination: to retain the ability to make decisions and take action independently. To be feared, in order to remain free,” French Armed Forces Minister Catherine Vautrin said during her speech inaugurating the Euronaval defense show today in Paris.
French President Emmanuel M acron has previously used similar words during his nuclear strategy address in March, when he announced in Brittany an increase in the country’s nuclear warhead stockpile. His message centered on a belief in strategic autonomy, and that to protect its sovereignty, Paris must remain a credible and feared power.
Vautrin made clear in her comments that naval power will be a prominent part in executing this vision. The first step: funding a naval drone effort, unveiled earlier this year that seeks to fast-track combining manned warships with autonomous systems.
According to the French Defence Procurement Agency (DGA), the initiative is structured across three categories: tactical drones intended particularly for escort and protection missions; endurance drones for intelligence and surveillance operations; and specialized action drones, which include remotely operated naval munitions. The total budget for these acquisitions has not been disclosed publicly, but likely won’t come cheap — part of why Macron’s government is looking to increase its overall defense spending.
“The draft budget I am presenting to parliament provides for defense spending to reach €63.4 billion in the 2027 financial year. That is €6.5 billion more than in 2026. This is historic,” Vautrin said.
The draft was presented to National Assembly and the Senate in October, but it has not yet been adopted. A vote is scheduled this month, while the draft is currently being debated widely within the French parliament.
During her speech, Vautrin also mentioned additional orders the DGA placed over the summer for surface and underwater drones under the French future mine-countermeasure program, known as SLAM-F. The French procurement arm ordered a dozen of these systems to bolster the French Navy’s uncrewed mine warfare capabilities, which it said are required to guarantee freedom of navigation in the current geopolitical context.
Vautrin also used her speech to underline that going forward Paris wants to prioritize buying systems of European origin.
“Our first weapon is our ability to manufacture as Europeans. That is how we will become stronger,” she said. “There are already successful examples: Greece … But I could also mention the quality and complementarity of our partnership with Sweden in the fields of missiles, aviation, and naval capabilities, with the objective of achieving mutual strategic autonomy. [Also] Belgium and the Netherlands, with our cooperation on new mine-warfare vessels.”

As fleets grow more diverse, reliable operational data—not algorithms—could decide how useful artificial intelligence (AI) becomes in the control room.
“If a 1-GW offshore wind park unexpectedly goes offline, the impact on grid stability can be significant,” Mark Robens, sales head for North and Western Europe for Controls & Digitalization at Siemens Energy, said as a guest on The POWER Podcast . That is why, Robens argued, renewables now belong in the same “critical infrastructure” category as large conventional power plants, and why the systems that control them must meet the same standard: trusted, secure, and reliable.
AI raises the stakes on that standard. Robens said the more digitalized and interconnected operations become, the more they depend on trusted control, because AI is only as useful as the operational data beneath it. Before AI can create value, he said, operators need a trusted operational foundation.
Orchestrating Systems, Not Assets
Power generation has become “more heterogeneous,” Robens said. Operators that once managed homogeneous fleets now run conventional generation alongside wind farms, solar plants, battery energy storage, and other distributed assets, all of which must work together to hold the grid steady. The technologies change, he said, but the requirement does not.
He pointed to a recent Siemens Energy project for a major energy company in South America. The customer runs a microgrid across multiple locations that combines gas turbines, wind generation, and battery storage. According to Robens, the challenge was not controlling any one asset but orchestrating an entire energy system: deciding when conventional generation should take over, when batteries should charge or discharge, and how to balance sustainability and reliability across a wide geographic area. The Omnivise T3000 control system provides the integrated operational layer for the site, he said.
Customers are increasingly asking about whole portfolios rather than individual units, Robens added. “They are no longer talking to us about a single asset; they are talking to us about a full portfolio of generation assets.”
Why Cybersecurity and Data Quality Come First
“There is a lot of excitement about AI right now, and I would say rightly so,” Robens said. “But AI is only as good as the information it has access to.” If operational data is incomplete, inconsistent, or stripped of context, he said, AI will not produce reliable recommendations.
Cybersecurity carries similar weight. As plants connect to external information technology systems and depend on digital applications, he said, the challenge grows, and security “can never be treated as an afterthought.” Robens said T3000 was designed to IEC 62443 and the ISO 27000 family of standards, which regulators increasingly reference for critical infrastructure. Whether the framework is NERC CIP in North America, KRITIS in Germany, or NIS regulations in Europe, he said, the expectation is the same.
From a Control Core to a Connected Ecosystem
Many plants have already digitalized, Robens said, but they often lack integration. Information sits in silos, applications run independently, and workflows still require manual intervention. Plants without a common, structured data foundation are limited in how well they can use AI, he said. “A power plant of the future will not be built on isolated systems. It will be built on connected intelligence.”
Siemens Energy’s answer is the Omnivise ecosystem, which Robens described as a framework that pools data from the expert applications running at a plant. He summarized the relationship between the two products as “control across, value above.” T3000 integrates assets horizontally across technologies and sites, he said, while the ecosystem extends vertically to connect operational data with applications, fleet operations, energy management, and market-facing processes. The ecosystem is vendor agnostic, he noted, and customers do not need T3000 to use it.
As an example of the ecosystem side, Robens cited EML S.A., a Portuguese energy company moving its renewable fleet from feed-in tariffs toward direct participation in energy markets. According to Siemens Energy, seven onshore wind farms totaling about 250 MW were connected through Omnivise T3000 Edge to a cloud-based operations and analytics environment. The setup gives EML a single interface for fleet monitoring, alarm handling, and supervisory control across all seven sites, providing the transparency needed to coordinate market dispatch in line with transmission system operator procedures. It will also support forecasting and dispatch and bid optimization, and the architecture is designed to extend to additional energy management functions and hybrid technologies such as solar and storage.
Practical AI, Not Replacement
Robens said AI’s value lies not in replacing operators but in helping them “make decisions faster” and “focus on higher value tasks.” Siemens Energy is working on AI-assisted root cause analysis, turbine tuning, incident response guidance, interactive manuals and reporting, and operational agents that give control room staff recommendations based on operating conditions. All of them, he said, depend on trusted, connected data.
Fully autonomous plants aren’t here yet, Robens acknowledged, but he said increasing levels of automation and autonomy are part of the industry’s future, and that AI is the key to getting there. Together with Volkswagen in Wolfsburg, Germany, Siemens Energy demonstrated 72 hours of unmanned operation at a power plant. That doesn’t mean an autonomous plant has arrived, Robens said, but it shows “where the industry is heading.”
